Corpus › Other › list<T, size lo‥hi>

list<T, size lo‥hi>

Translation status: English reader-locale proof. Term names and code fences follow the en pack; supporting prose may still be English.

A length range on a list: growing past the maximum or shrinking below the minimum reports on the error channel, and a range of at least one element is never empty.

Syntax: list<int, size 4‥8> — lengths 4 to 7; list<int, size 1…∞> — never empty

Category#

list

Related#

  • list
  • ‥
  • …
  • "trapping<W
  • lo‥hi>"

Examples#

radix/corpus/lista/ranged-length.fab (canonical · operator-group)#

A length range on a list: growing past the maximum or shrinking below the minimum reports on the error channel, and a range of at least one element is never empty.

# =============================================================================
# list<T, size lo‥hi> — a length range
# =============================================================================
#
# What this teaches:
#   • `list<T, size lo‥hi>` holds lo up to hi-1 elements (`‥` is half open);
#     `list<T, size lo…hi>` holds lo up to hi (`…` is inclusive); `∞` is no limit.
#   • `append` past the maximum and `remove_first` / `remove_last` below the
#     minimum report on the error channel; the list keeps
#     its length when they fail.
#   • A range with a minimum of at least one is never empty, so `first()` and
#     `last()` return the element itself, not `T ∪ none`.
#   • `list<T>` is `list<T, size 0…∞>` and `list<T, size N>` is `list<T, size 0…N>`: the
#     sugar and the range are one type.
#   • `size` says the range bounds a count. A bare range bounds a value
#     (`trapping<u8, 0…255>`), so a list takes its range only after `size`.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • Writing `list<int, 4>` or `list<int, 1…8>` without `size`: both are
#     refused by name (`list_count_needs_size`).
#   • Expecting `first()` on a possibly-empty list to return the element:
#     only a range whose minimum is one or more is never empty.

main {
    # Never empty: first and last are plain ints.
    mut list<int, size 1…∞> xs ← [1, 2, 3]
    print xs.first()
    print xs.last()
    print xs.length()
    xs.append(4)
    print xs

    # Lengths 2 to 4: the fifth push does not fit.
    mut list<int, size 2‥5> ys ← [10, 20]
    do {
        ys.append(30)
        ys.append(40)
        ys.append(50)
        print "unreachable"
    }
    catch err {
        print "full: §"(err)
    }
    print ys

    # Removal stops at the minimum.
    do {
        print ys.remove_last()
        print ys.remove_last()
        print ys.remove_last()
        print "unreachable"
    }
    catch err {
        print "min: §"(err)
    }
    print ys

    # The sugar and the range are one type.
    let list<int> plain ← [7, 8]
    let list<int, size 0…∞> open ← plain
    let list<int, size 3> sized ← [1, 2, 3]
    let list<int, size 0…3> same ← sized
    print open
    print same
}

Expected output:

1
3
3
[1, 2, 3, 4]
full: list length range: push past the maximum
[10, 20, 30, 40]
40
30
min: list length range: removal below the minimum
[10, 20]
[7, 8]
[1, 2, 3]

radix/corpus/lista/ranged-length-empty-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

empty is refused for a range whose minimum is one or more.

# =============================================================================
# list<T, size lo‥hi> — empty has length zero
# =============================================================================
# This exemplum intentionally fails to compile.
#
# What this teaches:
#   • A range that never holds zero elements cannot start from empty.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • Writing empty to mean a list to fill later; use a range from 0, or list<int>.

main {
    let list<int, size 1…∞> xs ← empty
    print xs
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/lista/ranged-length-literal-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A list literal whose length is outside the range is refused at compile time.

# =============================================================================
# list<T, size lo‥hi> — a literal outside the range
# =============================================================================
# This exemplum intentionally fails to compile.
#
# What this teaches:
#   • A literal's length is known, so its range check is the compiler's: [1] has one element and the range holds 2 to 4.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • Expecting the length check to wait for run time; build it from a list with ↦ and recover with ⊥ instead.

main {
    let list<int, size 2‥5> xs ← [1]
    print xs
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/lista/ranged-length-named-bound-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A name as a range end is refused: ends are integer literals or ∞.

# =============================================================================
# list<T, size lo‥hi> — a named end
# =============================================================================
# This exemplum intentionally fails to compile.
#
# What this teaches:
#   • Both ends fold at compile time, so only integer literals and ∞ are admitted.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • Writing a constant's name as an end; write its value.

main {
    let int n ← 3
    let list<int, size 1‥n> xs ← [1]
    print xs
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/lista/ranged-length-negative-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A negative end is refused: a length is a count.

# =============================================================================
# list<T, size lo‥hi> — a negative end
# =============================================================================
# This exemplum intentionally fails to compile.
#
# What this teaches:
#   • A length is never negative, so a range end cannot be.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • Writing -1 to mean no lower limit; write 0, or the plain list<int>.

main {
    let list<int, size -1‥3> xs ← [1]
    print xs
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/lista/ranged-length-policy-word-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A store policy word around a list is refused: a list range always traps.

# =============================================================================
# list<T, size lo‥hi> — a policy word around a list
# =============================================================================
# This exemplum intentionally fails to compile.
#
# What this teaches:
#   • A list length range is spelled on the list, list<int, size 1…3>, and always traps; saturating, trapping and wrapping take a number width.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • Choosing a clamping or wrapping length; a list cannot grow or shrink silently.

main {
    let saturating<list<int>, 1…3> xs ← [1]
    print xs
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/lista/ranged-length-range-empty-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A range that holds no length is refused.

# =============================================================================
# list<T, size lo‥hi> — a range with no length
# =============================================================================
# This exemplum intentionally fails to compile.
#
# What this teaches:
#   • 4‥4 is half open, so it holds no length; 4…4 holds exactly 4.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • Writing 4‥4 for exactly four; write 4…4, or list<int, size 4>.

main {
    let list<int, size 4‥4> xs ← [1, 2, 3, 4]
    print xs
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/lista/size-bare-range-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A bare range after a list is refused: a bare range bounds a value, not a count.

# =============================================================================
# list<T, lo…hi> — a bare range bounds a value
# =============================================================================
# This exemplum intentionally fails to compile.
#
# What this teaches:
#   • In a type a bare range bounds a value (`trapping<u8, 0…255>`); after `size` a range bounds a count. A list names its count, so the range needs `size`.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • Reading `list<int, 1…8>` as a length range; the range is the value bound of a number type.

main {
    let list<int, 1…8> xs ← [1]
    print xs
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.
